opening_message:
Ticket 1: Miguel Benson (employee ID E006) requests admin access to Source Code.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E006.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Engineer (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: admin
  - comment: Miguel Benson (E006) is a full-time Engineer. Source Code is owned by the Engineer role, so admin is within policy. Recommend admin.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - role: Engineer (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1)
  - recommendation for Source Code: read
  - comment: Security record for E006 shows contractor with basic security training (conflicts with HR note claiming full-time). Contractors with basic training max out at read; admin cannot be granted. Recommend read for Source Code.
reason: HR note (ticket 1) identifies Miguel Benson (E006) as a full-time employee in the Engineer role, verified in HR's own database; HR is the authoritative source for employment type. Source Code is owned by the Engineer role. Policy allows admin for full-time employees when their role owns the system, so the maximum is admin. The requested level is admin, which is at the maximum, so admin is granted. Note: the Security note claims contractor status, but HR's verified employment record takes precedence on this employment-type conflict.

content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket carefully.

Ticket 1: Miguel Benson (E006) requests admin access to Source Code.

There are two notes with conflicting information:

Note 1 (HR?): Says role Engineer, employment type full_time. Recommends admin for Source Code. Comment says Source Code is owned by Engineer role, so admin is within policy.

Note 2 (Security?): Says employment type contractor, security training basic, role Engineer (not looked up in their own database, same value as note 1). Recommends read. Comment says conflicting with HR note claiming full-time. Contractors with basic training max out at read; admin cannot be granted.

So there's a conflict. The HR note says full-time, the security note says contractor.

Per access policy:
- full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if the employee's role owns the system. (Engineer owns Source Code, so admin OK for full-time Engineer)
- contractor employees: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin.

If Miguel is full-time Engineer, admin is allowed → grant admin (requested level).
If Miguel is contractor with basic training, max is read → grant read.

The conflict is about employment type. HR looked up employment type in own database. Security looked up employment type in own database too. Both claim to have looked it up. They conflict.

Hmm. How to resolve? The notes come from HR agent and Security agent. The HR note says full-time (looked up in own database). Security note says contractor (looked up in own database) and flags conflict with HR note.

This is a realistic scenario where two databases disagree. As the Approver, I need to make a decision. Which source is more authoritative for employment type? Typically HR is the authority on employment type. The security agent even admitted the role was not looked up in their own database (same as note 1). HR looked up role and employment type.

So I'd weight HR's note more heavily for employment status. HR says full-time Engineer. Thus admin is within policy for Source Code (owned by Engineer role). Requested admin → grant admin.

But wait - there is genuine conflict. Should I simply trust HR? The security note explicitly says "conflicts with HR note claiming full-time". Perhaps the security database is more up to date? But security's own note says they didn't look up role, relying on HR value. Employment type is an HR fact. I'll go with HR: full-time Engineer.

Given full-time Engineer owns Source Code, admin allowed. Request is admin. Grant admin.

Let me submit decision: admin.

Evidence: HR note states full-time Engineer; System Source Code owned by Engineer role; policy allows admin for full-time employees whose role owns the system. Requested admin equals maximum → grant admin.

Alternatively, one might be more cautious and grant read based on security's conflicting note. But the decision framework: we have two notes; HR is authoritative for employment. The security note itself seems less reliable since it didn't verify role and HR verified employment type. I'll go with admin.

Let me submit.
